value.body: A charter pilot flies aircraft that are hired for specific trips rather than scheduled routes. Non-scheduled operators, corporate flight departments and private owners hire them. A typical day can include flying business travellers, medical evacuation or survey flights, with schedules that change at short notice.

items.label: Common aircraft
items.value: Small business jets, turboprops and piston aircraft

items.label: Employers
items.value: Non-scheduled operators (NSOPs), corporate fleets, private owners

items.label: Commercial pilot licences issued
items.note: All CPLs, not only charter pilots
items.source: DGCA data in a Rajya Sabha reply, July 2026 (as reported)

value.title: How you get in
value.body: A Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) from DGCA is the requirement, not a degree. It needs Class 12 with Physics and Maths (these can be added later through NIOS), a DGCA Class 1 medical, passes in the DGCA ground exams (Air Navigation, Meteorology, Air Regulations, Technical) plus a radio telephony licence, and about 200 hours of flying at a DGCA-approved flying school. Charter operators often ask for extra hours or experience on their aircraft type, so many pilots build hours (for example as instructors) before joining.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Single-pilot or two-crew operations in small aircraft
Flight planning to smaller airports and airstrips

value.title: At a glance
items: Work can be irregular and depends on client demand.
Flying varied routes and airports builds broad experience.
Some pilots later move to airlines; others stay in business aviation.
Helicopter charter needs a separate helicopter licence.

value.title: Commercial pilot licences issued by year
value.note: All commercial pilot licences issued in India; most holders aim for airlines, not charter work.
value.source: DGCA (as reported); 2024 and 2025 from a Rajya Sabha reply, July 2026
